sections.text: Two percentage discounts do not add up. A sign that says 30 percent off plus an extra 20 percent off gives you 44 percent off, not 50, because the second discount is taken from the already-reduced price. On a 100 dollar item the first discount leaves 70 dollars, and 20 percent of 70 is 14, so you pay 56. The shortfall of 6 percentage points is the stacking gap, and it is pure arithmetic: each discount multiplies the price by (1 - rate).

items: Final price = original price x (1 - d1) x (1 - d2) x ... where each d is a decimal (20 percent is 0.20).
Effective discount = 1 - (1 - d1) x (1 - d2) x ...
Sale tax, if applied after the discounts, = final price x tax rate.

sections.text: The Percent Off Calculator applies up to two stacked discounts followed by a sales tax rate, and it shows the stacking gap against the simple sum. It treats tax as a final step on the discounted price, which matches many ordinary retail checkouts but not every case.
Each row below starts from 100 dollars, so the final price is also the percentage of the original you still pay.

Two patterns are worth remembering. The gap grows as the discounts get larger, and it is biggest when both are large. And for percentage-only stacks, order does not matter: 20 percent then 10 percent gives 72, and so does 10 percent then 20 percent, because multiplication gives the same product in either order.

Take an item listed at 129.99 dollars, with 30 percent off and an extra 20 percent off at the register, and a sales tax rate of 7.5 percent. The tax rate is an illustrative assumption; use your local rate.

The effective discount is 44.0 percent, the same as in the table above, because it depends only on the two rates and not on the price. Intermediate values are rounded to cents for display; the totals use unrounded numbers and agree to the cent.
Order does matter when you mix a percentage with a fixed-dollar coupon. On a 100 dollar item with 20 percent off and a 10 dollar coupon:

Taking the percentage first and the coupon second is cheaper for you by 2 dollars, because the coupon then removes a full 10 dollars from a smaller number. The difference equals the percentage applied to the coupon value (20 percent of 10). Which order a retailer applies is decided by its own terms, so read the coupon conditions.

items: Find the original price from a sale price: divide by (1 - discount). An item that costs 63 dollars at 30 percent off was 63 / 0.70 = 90 dollars.
With two stacked discounts, divide by both factors. Paying 56 dollars after 30 percent and 20 percent means the original price was 56 / (0.70 x 0.80) = 100 dollars.

Restoring a price takes a larger percentage than the discount. A 20 percent discount must be reversed by a 25 percent increase, a 30 percent discount by 42.9 percent, and a 50 percent discount by 100 percent.

sections.text: To compare deals, convert each to an effective discount. A 30 percent plus 20 percent stack (44.0 percent effective) loses to a flat 45 percent off. To reach 50 percent off after a first 30 percent discount, the second discount would need to be 28.57 percent, since 1 - 0.50 / 0.70 = 0.2857. Quantity deals convert the same way: buy two get the third free is a 33.3 percent saving per item, and buy one get one at 50 percent off is 25 percent on the pair.

items: Adding discount percentages together instead of multiplying them.

Assuming tax is calculated on the original price. Check whether your retailer taxes the discounted amount, since some coupons are treated differently from price reductions depending on the place, and rules vary.
Judging a sale by the percentage alone. A larger discount on an inflated list price can cost more than a smaller discount on a fair one.
Forgetting that rounding at each step can move the total by a cent.

sections.text: This guide covers arithmetic only. Sales tax rules, coupon rules and advertising rules differ by place and retailer, so confirm anything that affects what you actually pay with the retailer or your local tax authority.

sections.heading: Stop Overpaying on Sales
sections.body: Use TheCalcUniverse Percent Off Calculator to see the true final price after stacked discounts and sales tax. No more getting fooled by misleading markdown math.
